text: Augusta Ada King, Countess of Lovelace (née Byron; 10 December 1815 – 27 November 1852), was an English mathematician and writer best known for her work on Charles Babbage's proposed mechanical general-purpose computer, the analytical engine. She was the first to recognize that the machine could have applications beyond pure calculation, and is often considered the first computer programmer. Lovelace was the only legitimate child of poet Lord Byron and reformer Anne Isabella Milbanke. Lord Byron separated from his wife a month after Ada was born and died when she was eight years old. Although often ill in childhood, including experiencing vision-obscuring headaches at age eight and paralysis from measles in 1829, she pursued her studies diligently. She married William King in 1835; King was a Baron, created Viscount Ockham and 1st Earl of Lovelace in 1838, and the title made Ada the Countess of Lovelace, as she was descended from the extinct Baron Lovelaces. Lovelace's educational and social connections included scientists such as Andrew Crosse, Charles Babbage, David Brewster, Charles Wheatstone, Michael Faraday, and author Charles Dickens, which she used to advance her knowledge. She described her approach as "poetical science" and referred to herself as an "Analyst (& Metaphysician)". At eighteen, she began a long working relationship with Charles Babbage, particularly interested in his analytical engine. She first met him on 5 June 1833 at a soirée with Mary Somerville, and later that month, Babbage invited her to see the prototype of his difference engine. Lovelace became fascinated with the machine and visited Babbage frequently through her connection with Somerville. Babbage admired her intellect and called her "The Enchantress of Number". In 1840, Babbage gave a seminar in Turin, and Luigi Menabrea transcribed it in French, which was published in 1842. Babbage's friend Charles Wheatstone commissioned Lovelace to translate Menabrea's paper into English. Over a nine-month period in 1842–43, she translated the article and added seven long explanatory notes, A to G, which were published in September 1843 under her initials AAL. Note G described a method for calculating Bernoulli numbers using the analytical engine, often regarded as the first published computer program. Lovelace was the first to suggest that computers could process information beyond numbers, such as music, and to consider the broader societal implications of technology. Her work was well received, with Michael Faraday describing himself as a supporter. Despite a minor falling out when Babbage tried to leave his statement unsigned and was forced to sign it, their friendship recovered. Lovelace died at age 36 on 27 November 1852 from cervical cancer (then referred to as uterine cancer). During her final illness, Lady Byron controlled who she saw, excluded her friends, and influenced her to repent and make Lady Byron her executor. She lost contact with her husband after confessing something to him on 30 August, the nature of which is unknown. She was buried next to her father at the Church of St. Mary Magdalene in Hucknall, Nottinghamshire. Lovelace had an affair with a tutor in early 1833, tried to elope, and the incident was covered up by her mother and friends. She had no close relationship with her mother, who often watched her closely and referred to her daughter as "it" in letters, and she dubbed the observers the "Furies". She had no relationship with her younger half-sister Allegra, who died in 1822 at age five, and avoided contact with Elizabeth Medora Leigh, daughter of Byron's half-sister Augusta Leigh. In 1841, her mother told her that Byron was also Medora's father, and Lovelace wrote that she had long suspected this, blaming Augusta Leigh for being more wicked than Byron. In the 1840s, she engaged in scandals involving extra-marital relationships and gambling, losing over £3,000 on horses and attempting to create a mathematical model for successful large bets in 1851, which ended in debt. She had a shadowy relationship with Andrew Crosse's son John from 1844 onward, and John destroyed their correspondence after her death, receiving her father's only heirlooms. She was privately educated in mathematics and science by William Frend, William King, and Mary Somerville, and later studied advanced calculus with Augustus De Morgan, who praised her potential as an original mathematical investigator. She often integrated poetry and science, writing to De Morgan about the "sprites and fairies" of mathematical transformations, and valued metaphysics as much as mathematics. In 1844, she expressed interest in creating a "calculus of the nervous system" and visited Andrew Crosse to learn about electrical experiments. She also wrote a review of Karl von Reichenbach's paper on magnetism, which was not published. In 1851, she mentioned "certain productions" on the relation of math and music. Lovelace and Babbage were reputed to have walked together on Philosopher's Walk at Worthy Manor while discussing mathematical principles. Her work on the analytical engine, though the machine was never built and did not influence electronic computers, is recognized as a Turing-complete general-purpose computer, and Babbage is known as the "father of computers" while Lovelace is credited with several computing "firsts". She is widely commemorated in programming languages, roads, buildings, institutes, and educational programs, as well as in plaques, statues, paintings, and literary works. Lord Byron expected a "glorious boy" and was disappointed when Lady Byron gave birth to a girl, named Ada after his half-sister Augusta Leigh. On 16 January 1816, at Byron's command, Lady Byron left for her parents' home with their five-week-old daughter. Although English law granted full custody to the father in separation, Byron made no attempt to claim parental rights and only requested that his sister be informed of Ada's welfare. He signed the deed of separation on 21 April and left England shortly after. Lady Byron continued to accuse him of immoral behavior, which made Lovelace infamous in Victorian society. She did not have a relationship with her father and was not shown a family portrait of him until her 20th birthday. Her mother was the only significant parental figure in her life. She had three children: Byron (1836), Anne Isabella (Annabella, 1837), and Ralph Gordon (1839). Immediately after Annabella's birth, Lady King suffered a prolonged illness. In 1843–44, her mother assigned William Benjamin Carpenter to teach her children and act as a moral instructor, but he fell for her and encouraged her to express frustrated affections; when it became clear he was trying to start an affair, she ended the relationship. From 1832, her mathematical abilities began to emerge, and her interest in mathematics dominated her adult life. She was taught mathematics early due to her mother's concerns about her potential madness. In 1841, her mother revealed that Byron was also Medora's father, and Lovelace wrote that she had long suspected it, blaming Augusta Leigh. She died from cervical cancer after several months of illness, during which Lady Byron restricted her access to friends and confidants. She requested to be buried next to her father.

Ada Lovelace's notes on Charles Babbage's Analytical Engine are significant in the early history of computing, particularly because Note G provides a complete and detailed method for calculating a sequence of Bernoulli numbers using the engine, which might have functioned correctly if the machine had been built. Although Babbage's personal notes from 1837 to 1840 contain the first programs for the engine, the algorithm in Note G is often recognized as the first published computer program. The Analytical Engine was never completed, so the program was never tested. In 1953, Lovelace's notes were republished as an appendix to B. V. Bowden's Faster than Thought, and the engine is now acknowledged as an early model for a computer, with her notes regarded as a description of a computer and software. Lovelace is frequently called the first computer programmer, and her method is described as the world's first computer program. However, Eugene Eric Kim and Betty Alexandra Toole consider it incorrect to regard her as the first computer programmer; Babbage claims credit in his autobiography for the algorithm in Note G, and he had written initial programs for the engine, with several dozen sample programs prepared between 1837 and 1840, all predating Lovelace's notes. Allan G. Bromley notes that all but one of the programs cited in her notes were prepared by Babbage three to seven years earlier, and there is no evidence that Ada ever wrote a program for the Analytical Engine; her correspondence with Babbage shows she lacked the necessary knowledge. Bruce Collier states that Lovelace made a considerable contribution to publicizing the engine but did not advance its design or theory. Doron Swade agrees that Ada only published the first computer program rather than writing it, but acknowledges she was the only person to see the potential of the engine as a machine capable of manipulating entities beyond numbers, such as letters or musical notes. Stephen Wolfram defends Lovelace's contributions, arguing that her computation of Bernoulli numbers is more sophisticated and clear than Babbage's, and that she distilled from Babbage's correspondence a clear exposition of the machine's abstract operations—something Babbage never did. In her notes, Lovelace emphasized the engine's ability to solve problems of any complexity, noting it could act upon objects whose fundamental relations could be expressed through operations, such as musical notes, and she wrote that the engine could compose music of any complexity. This insight, inspired by observing mechanical looms using punchcards, anticipated modern computing by a century. She also dismissed the idea of artificial intelligence, stating the engine has no ability to originate anything or anticipate analytical truths—a view debated by Alan Turing and now considered outdated by most modern computer scientists. Lovelace distinguished between the mechanical details of the Difference Engine (covered in an 1834 article) and the logical structure of the Analytical Engine, noting both aspects were equally essential. The computer language Ada, created by the U.S. Department of Defense, was named after her; its reference manual was approved on 10 December 1980, and its military standard, MIL-STD-1815, was assigned the year of her birth. In 1981, the Association for Women in Computing established the Ada Lovelace Award; the British Computer Society has awarded the Lovelace Medal since 1998 and initiated an annual competition for women students in 2008, and sponsors the Lovelace Colloquium. In 2013, the University of Deusto in Spain established the Ada Byron Award for women in technology, later expanding it to several Latin American countries. Ada, the National College for Digital Skills, has campuses in London and Manchester and offers degree-level apprenticeships and sixth-form education. Ada Lovelace Day is celebrated annually on the second Tuesday of October, beginning in 2009, to raise the profile of women in science, technology, engineering, and maths and to create role models for girls and women, including Wikipedia edit-a-thons to reduce gender bias. The Ada Initiative promoted women's involvement in free culture and open source movements. The Engineering Mathematics department at the University of Bristol is named the Ada Lovelace Building; the Engineering in Computer Science and Telecommunications College at Zaragoza University is named the Ada Byron Building; the computer centre in Porlock is named after her; and Ada Lovelace House is a council-owned building near where she spent her infancy. In 2012, a Google Doodle and blog post honored her on her birthday; in 2013, Ada Developers Academy was founded to diversify tech by training women and gender-diverse individuals as software developers. On 17 September 2013, the BBC Radio 4 programme Great Lives featured a biography of Lovelace, sponsored by Konnie Huq. As of November 2015, all new British passports include an illustration of Lovelace and Babbage. In 2017, a Google Doodle honored her on International Women's Day with other women. On 2 February 2018, Satellogic launched a micro-satellite named in her honor. In March 2018, The New York Times published a belated obituary. On 27 July 2018, Senator Ron Wyden introduced a U.S. Senate resolution designating 9 October 2018 as National Ada Lovelace Day, which passed unanimously. In November 2020, Trinity College Dublin announced it would commission four new busts of women, one of whom was Lovelace, unveiled on 1 February 2023. In March 2022, a statue of Ada Lovelace was installed at the former Ergon House in London, sculpted by Etienne and Mary Millner and based on a portrait by Margaret Sarah Carpenter, unveiled on International Women's Day, 2022, on the 7th floor of Millbank Quarter. In September 2022, Nvidia announced the Ada Lovelace graphics processing unit microarchitecture. In July 2023, the Royal Mint issued four £2 commemorative coins honoring Lovelace and her legacy. In 2025, the National Portrait Gallery acquired three known photographs of Lovelace—two daguerreotypes by Antoine Claudet taken around 1843 and one by an unknown photographer, believed to be from Henry Wyndham Phillips’ portrait. Events in 2025 celebrated the bicentenary of her birth, including special exhibitions at the Science Museum in London and the Weston Library in Oxford. Lovelace is portrayed in Romulus Linney's 1977 play Childe Byron, Tom Stoppard's 1993 play Arcadia (where Thomasina Coverly is "apparently based" on her), the 1990 steampunk novel The Difference Engine (where she delivers a lecture proving Gödel's theorems), Jordan Stratford's The Wollstonecraft Detective Agency, John Crowley's 2005 novel Lord Byron's Novel: The Evening Land, the 2015 play Ada and the Engine, and the webcomic and graphic novel The Thrilling Adventures of Lovelace and Babbage, which includes extensive footnotes and dialogue from actual correspondence. In the 1997 film Conceiving Ada, a computer scientist communicates with her through "undying information waves." In the 2017 ITV series The Frankenstein Chronicles, Lily Lesser portrays her as an analyst working on a humanoid automaton with brass workings reminiscent of the Analytical Engine. In the 2015 AMC series Halt and Catch Fire, "Lovelace" is the name of a fictional operating system. In the 2015 documentary Calculating Ada: The Countess of Computing, Dr Hannah Fry covers her life. In the 2017 ITV series Victoria, Emerald Fennell portrays her in the episode "The Green-Eyed Monster." In the 2020 Doctor Who episode "Spyfall, Part 2," Sylvie Briggs plays her alongside Charles Babbage and Noor Inayat Khan. Six copies of the 1843 first edition of Sketch of the Analytical Engine with Lovelace's notes have been located: three at Harvard University, one at the University of Oklahoma, one at the U.S. Air Force Academy, and the sixth sold at auction on 20 July 2018 for £95,000 to an anonymous buyer. A digital facsimile of one copy from Harvard University is available online. In December 2016, a letter written by Lovelace was forfeited by Martin Shkreli to the New York State Department of Taxation and Finance for unpaid taxes.

Ace appears as a character in "Spyfall, Part 2," the second episode of Doctor Who, series 12, which first aired on BBC One on 5 January 2020. The character is portrayed by Sylvie Briggs, alongside performances by Charles Babbage and Noor Inayat Khan. Six copies of the 1843 first edition of Sketch of the Analytical Engine with Ada Lovelace's "Notes" have been identified; three are held at Harvard University, one at the University of Oklahoma, and one at the United States Air Force Academy. On 20 July 2018, the sixth copy was sold at auction to an anonymous buyer for £95,000. A digital facsimile of one of the copies housed in the Harvard University Library is accessible online. In December 2016, a letter written by Ada Lovelace was forfeited by Martin Shkreli to the New York State Department of Taxation and Finance due to unpaid taxes owed by Shkreli.
